newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela offers to share power with Zulu chief.
newsitem.headline: Mandela offers to share power with Zulu chief.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela is wooing his main black rival, Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, with the offer of a seat in a ruling triumvirate, government and party sources said on Monday.
"There are a number of options for Mr Buthelezi, but the main one on offer is to make him a deputy president alongside Deputy President (Thabo) Mbeki," a senior government source told Reuters.

A source in the ruling African National Congress (ANC) said Buthelezi, currently minister of home affairs in the national unity coalition, was interested in the proposal, but had not yet set terms or discussed the offer with Mandela.
The offer is part of a peace plan proposed by the ANC to end more than a decade of conflict with Buthelezi's Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) in KwaZulu-Natal province.

The plan includes a special arrangement to include IFP and ANC combatants in the award by Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission of amnesty for politically motivated human rights violations during the apartheid years.

Buthelezi has so far refused to cooperate with the TRC and said in a radio interview on Monday that he would rather face prison. "If they want to jail me they can go ahead. I am not prepared (to cooperate)," he said.
He said in a statement earlier he had not discussed the ANC's offer of a post as deputy president with Mandela, adding:
"I am not prepared to comment on any aspect of the peace package or to respond to kites which are being flown about my possible future political position."
The ANC said in a statement the offer should be seen only as a bid to secure peace in KwaZulu-Natal, where more than 20,000 people have died in a decade of conflict with the IFP.
"The ANC welcomes the broad thrust of the proposal as a genuine effort to find lasting solutions to the problems of KwaZulu-Natal," the party said.
The offer to Buthelezi is the latest move in a nascent political realignment ahead of South Africa's second democratic election in 1999.

Former president F.W. de Klerk gave up a position as deputy president alongside Mbeki when he pulled his National Party out of the unity government last year and now his white-led party is seeking allies, possibly including the IFP, to fight the dominance of the ANC in 1999.

Former NP strategist Roelf Meyer, who quit last month in a row with de Klerk, said at the weekend that he and expelled ANC dissident Bantu Holomisa, who has significant support among disaffected ANC members, might form a new political party soon.
Democratic Party leader Tony Leon, who has also been in talks with the Inkatha leader, said there were signs that a shake-up in South African politics was imminent.
"It's starting to happen and I think it is to be welcomed. I think the old divisions will give way to new and hopefully more realistic ones," he said.
